anchor.summary: A 2026 survey of agentic CI/CD that identifies 'authority transfer' — how much operational control you hand an AI agent — as the open, unsolved problem in this space, and states that no explicit boundary or benchmark for it exists yet.

corePapers.summary: Industrial-scale proof this category of tool works: ran on 1M+ real ByteDance pipeline runs with over 80% precision. Does not distinguish file risk.
Treats the LLM as an agent that investigates a bug using tools, not just a single-shot patch generator. Same blind spot: no concept of file risk.

corePapers.role: Proof the risk is real, not hypothetical
corePapers.summary: A real bot that watched GitHub CI builds and got patches merged by humans — some of whom didn't know it was a bot. Shows autonomous agents already have real merge power with zero classification of what they're allowed to touch.
A self-healing layer for DevSecOps pipelines, but narrow (security anomalies only) and driven by a learned reinforcement-learning policy rather than a declarative, auditable rule.

supportingCluster.role: Grounds the HOW, not the WHAT/WHY
supportingCluster.summary: Twelve additional sources on trust calibration, human-AI collaboration, policy-as-code, and infrastructure security. Not CI/CD-specific — they justify design choices like confidence-based routing, keeping a human in the loop, and using declarative policy instead of a black-box model.
